The model predicted a 65% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year grades had the strongest influence, followed by your family income bracket, and then your undergraduate GPA. All three pushed the prediction toward failure rather than success.

Your performance placed you in the third decile for third-year grades, noticeably below the average of accepted students. This lower academic standing in later law school years signaled to the model a higher risk of struggling with the bar exam. Your family being in the upper-middle income bracket also contributed to the negative outlook, as this group is associated with slightly higher failure rates in the data the model learned from. Finally, your undergraduate GPA of 2.90 fell short of the 3.23 average among accepted applicants, further increasing the predicted likelihood of not passing the bar.

Taken together, these academic and background signals led the model to conclude you were more likely to fail than succeed.

You should focus on strengthening your academic record, perhaps by excelling in any remaining coursework, seeking targeted bar exam preparation, or gaining practical legal experience that could demonstrate your readiness. Reapplying with improved indicators in these key areas could meaningfully change future predictions. (218 words)
